reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A malformation of cortical development due to arrested neuronal migration, producing a smooth brain surface with absent (agyria) or reduced and broadened (pachygyria) gyri
MRI shows a thickened, poorly organised cortex, a smooth grey-white junction, and often a characteristic figure-of-eight or hourglass appearance in severe classic forms
Classic type I lissencephaly is commonly caused by LIS1 (PAFAH1B1) deletions or variants, giving a posterior-predominant (posterior worse than anterior) gradient of malformation
DCX variants are X-linked and cause anterior-predominant lissencephaly in hemizygous males and subcortical band heterotopia (double cortex) in heterozygous females
Miller-Dieker syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion at 17p13.3 involving LIS1, combining severe lissencephaly with a distinctive facial appearance
Children typically present with early hypotonia, feeding difficulty, profound developmental delay, and drug-resistant epilepsy including infantile spasms
Diagnosis relies on the MRI malformation pattern and gradient combined with targeted or panel-based molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Lissencephaly results from failure of the tangential and radial migration of neurons from the germinal zones to the developing cortical plate during the first half of gestation. Variants in genes that regulate the microtubule cytoskeleton and motor-driven nucleokinesis, most notably LIS1 and DCX, impair neuronal movement so that neurons arrest before reaching their proper cortical layers. The cortex becomes abnormally thick and disorganised with few or no gyri, and the anteroposterior gradient of severity reflects the particular gene involved. Disrupted cortical architecture underlies the profound epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly of the dystroglycanopathies such as Walker-Warburg syndrome
Subcortical band heterotopia and other heterotopias
Tubulinopathies from TUBA1A and related genes
Congenital infection causing a migration-like disturbance
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to define the gyral pattern, cortical thickness, and anteroposterior severity gradient
Molecular genetic testing including LIS1 and DCX analysis and a cortical malformation panel
Chromosomal microarray to detect 17p13.3 deletion in suspected Miller-Dieker syndrome
Electroencephalography to characterise the epilepsy, including hypsarrhythmia
Genetic counselling and, where relevant, testing of parents for mosaicism or carrier status
redFlags: Drug-resistant epilepsy including infantile spasms causing developmental regression
Recurrent aspiration and failure to thrive from bulbar dysfunction
Progressive respiratory compromise in severe forms
Facial dysmorphism suggesting Miller-Dieker syndrome that warrants microarray testing
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor in severe classic lissencephaly, with profound intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and often shortened survival due to respiratory and feeding complications. Milder pachygyria and band heterotopia can be associated with better cognitive and seizure outcomes.
pitfalls: Confusing classic lissencephaly with cobblestone lissencephaly, which has different genetics and eye and muscle involvement
Overlooking subcortical band heterotopia in a mother of an affected child, missing X-linked DCX inheritance
Failing to arrange microarray testing when facial features suggest Miller-Dieker syndrome
Underestimating the anteroposterior gradient as a clue to the causative gene
